value.title: Campaign readiness: faster, more reliable redirects, trustworthy probes, stats and docs for the URL shortener (single-instance SQLite, 50 RPS / p95 < 100 ms)
value.problem_statement:
Next week marketing launches a billboard and TV campaign that puts our short links in front of the public. The product owner has set the targets. Peak load is modest, up to about 50 redirect requests per second. Redirect latency must have p95 under 100 ms. Availability is best effort on a single instance. Production stays on SQLite, hardened with WAL, a busy_timeout and a configurable pool. No new database driver is added, and the move to PostgreSQL for multi-worker or larger scale is documented, not implemented.

The current service has defects that make it slow or untrustworthy under campaign traffic:
(1) On SQLite, redirect lookups block behind click and create commits. There is no WAL and the busy timeout is the default 5 s, so a failed lookup becomes a 503. The runbook wrongly says redirects still return 307 in this case.
(2) The connection pool is fixed at 5+10 with a 30 s checkout timeout and cannot be configured.
(3) HEAD /healthz and HEAD /readyz are caught by the catch-all HEAD /{code} route and return 404 'Link not found', so HEAD-based uptime monitors will report an outage.
(4) Stats memory and time grow with every click, so a campaign-scale link could make the endpoint very slow or exhaust worker memory.
(5) On MySQL, case-sensitive codes are matched case-insensitively. This is a lower priority now that production stays on SQLite.
(6) The docs contradict the code on authentication and leave out API_KEY.

This change makes the redirect path fast and resistant to write contention on one SQLite instance, makes database tuning configurable, makes the probes and analytics trustworthy, and corrects the docs, including campaign deployment guidance and the PostgreSQL migration path. Every existing contract must stay intact: the 307 with the exact Location header and no-store, the immediate 410 after deactivation, synchronous click counting, privacy, and the architecture rules. With a one-week deadline, the scope favours small, low-risk changes at the database and engine level over caching, asynchronous ingestion, schema changes or new drivers. New requirement ids continue from the existing FR-1..FR-13 and NFR-1..NFR-9.

functional.title: HEAD support on liveness and readiness probes
functional.description: /healthz and /readyz must answer HEAD requests themselves instead of falling through to the catch-all HEAD /{code} redirect route. This fixes the existing defect where HEAD /healthz and HEAD /readyz return 404 'Link not found'. External uptime monitors for the campaign commonly probe with HEAD.
acceptance_criteria: HEAD /healthz returns 200 with an empty body and does not touch the database. Test: the app uses a session factory that raises on use, and the request still returns 200.
HEAD /readyz returns 200 with an empty body when SELECT 1 succeeds.
HEAD /readyz returns 503 when the readiness DB check fails. The 503 comes from the readiness check, not from a link lookup, and the response contains no exception text, SQL or stack trace.
No links-table lookup runs for HEAD /healthz or HEAD /readyz, verified by counting SQL statements or by spying on LinkRepository.
GET /healthz and GET /readyz keep their current status codes and JSON bodies.
POST /healthz and POST /readyz still return 405.

HEAD /{code} for any other code is unchanged: 307 with the exact Location and Cache-Control: no-store for active links; 404 JSON for unknown or malformed codes; 410 JSON with no Location for deactivated links; no click recorded.
The redirect router is still included last. The set of OpenAPI paths and named schemas is unchanged, and HEAD /{code} stays out of the schema.

functional.title: Redirects resilient to database write contention (hardened SQLite)
functional.description: A held write lock or a failed click write must not stall or fail the public redirect beyond a bounded, configurable time. For file-based SQLite, every new connection enables WAL journal mode, synchronous=NORMAL and a configurable busy_timeout, so readers do not block behind click or create commits. Click recording stays synchronous and best-effort. If the click INSERT or COMMIT fails or times out, the transaction is rolled back, a log line without any IP is written, and the visitor still gets the 307.
acceptance_criteria: New setting SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS: an integer from 0 to 60000, default 5000 (the current pysqlite behaviour). A value outside the range fails settings validation at startup with a clear error.

For a file-based SQLite DATABASE_URL, any connection taken from the engine reports PRAGMA journal_mode = 'wal', PRAGMA synchronous = 1 (NORMAL), and PRAGMA busy_timeout equal to SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS.
For in-memory SQLite URLs ('sqlite://' and ':memory:'), the app starts and serves requests without error; WAL is either not applied or its failure is tolerated.
Non-SQLite engines get no SQLite pragmas and keep pool_pre_ping=True. SQLite keeps check_same_thread=False.

Lock test setup: a temp file database, SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS=200, and a second connection holding a write lock (BEGIN IMMEDIATE with an uncommitted insert). Under these conditions, GET /{code} for an active link returns 307 with the exact Location within 700 ms (200 ms + 500 ms). No click is persisted for that request, and exactly one warning log line without the IP is emitted.
With the same write lock held, HEAD /{code} returns 307 and GET /{code} for a deactivated link returns 410. WAL means the lookup is not blocked.
With no lock held, exactly one click_event is persisted per successful GET, and total_clicks reflects it immediately after the response (synchronous visibility is preserved).

If the link lookup itself cannot run because the database is unavailable, the redirect returns 503 JSON {"detail": ...} with no internal details. docs/OPERATIONS.md describes this accurately and no longer claims that redirects always return 307 under 'database is locked'.

functional.title: Configurable database connection pool
functional.description: Pool sizing must be configurable through validated settings, so operators can size the pool for campaign load on the single SQLite instance and later on PostgreSQL. The defaults reproduce today's SQLAlchemy behaviour.
acceptance_criteria: New settings: DB_POOL_SIZE (integer ≥1, default 5), DB_MAX_OVERFLOW (integer ≥0, default 10), DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS (number >0 and ≤300, default 30).
An invalid value (for example DB_POOL_SIZE=0, DB_MAX_OVERFLOW=-1 or DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS=0) fails settings validation with a clear error, and the app does not start.
For file-based SQLite and non-SQLite URLs (QueuePool), engine.pool.size() equals DB_POOL_SIZE, and the pool's overflow and timeout match the settings.
In-memory SQLite URLs ignore the pool settings without error.
Existing settings defaults are unchanged. test_settings_defaults_and_env is extended, not weakened.
The engine and pool are still created per app inside create_app and stored on app.state. There is no module-level engine, settings object or pool.

functional.title: Lean redirect query budget
functional.description: The redirect hot path must do the minimum database work: a narrow lookup by code of only the columns it needs (id, url, is_active), plus a click insert for GET only. This supports the p95 < 100 ms campaign target.
acceptance_criteria: A successful GET /{code} issues exactly one SELECT on links (selecting only the needed columns), one INSERT into click_events and one COMMIT, verified by a SQLAlchemy before_cursor_execute event counter.
HEAD /{code} issues exactly one SELECT and no INSERT.
A malformed code (one that fails ^[A-Za-z0-9]{1,32}$) issues no SQL and returns 404 JSON.
A lookup of an unknown or deactivated code issues one SELECT and no INSERT.
The Location header stays byte-identical to the stored URL (no re-quoting).

functional.title: Bounded-memory stats aggregation
functional.description: GET /api/links/{code}/stats must not load one Python object per click. Daily buckets must be aggregated in SQL, or streamed with constant memory, so memory is proportional to the number of days rather than the number of clicks. Response semantics are unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: The repository no longer returns a list of per-click timestamps. At any one time, the stats path holds at most one row per day in the window plus at most one row per distinct referrer group (or streams with yield_per). A unit test on the repository's return shape verifies this.

Semantics are unchanged:
- UTC-day bucketing, including clicks on either side of UTC midnight.
- The days=1..365 window includes today.
- Empty days are omitted, and days are in ascending order.
- Totals are all-time.
- Referrers are ordered by count descending, then referrer ascending, with NULL last on ties, capped at the top 10.
- Missing or empty referrers are grouped as NULL.
- days outside 1..365 keep the existing error contract (422).
All existing tests in tests/test_stats.py pass unmodified, including test_day_bucketing_across_utc_midnight and the fixed-now service test.
Any dialect-specific date expression is guarded per dialect (SQLite, PostgreSQL, MySQL). A test compiles the SQL for all three dialects without needing an external driver connection.

With 200,000 clicks seeded on one link in a temp SQLite file, GET /stats?days=365 returns 200 in under 2 s, and the tracemalloc peak during the call is at most 2× the peak with 2,000 clicks. This test is marked slow.

functional.title: Case-sensitive short-code matching on MySQL
functional.description: Short codes are case-sensitive base62. On MySQL, the links.code column must use a binary or case-sensitive collation for fresh databases, and the docs must give the manual DDL for existing deployments. Q-2 confirmed that production stays on SQLite, so this is a portability fix and not a campaign blocker.
acceptance_criteria: CreateTable(Link.__table__) compiled with the MySQL dialect declares links.code with a case-sensitive or binary collation (for example utf8mb4_bin).
The compiled DDL for SQLite and PostgreSQL is unchanged from before.
docs/OPERATIONS.md contains the exact ALTER TABLE statement for existing MySQL databases and explains why it is needed.
On SQLite, /AbC1234 and /abc1234 still resolve independently (existing behaviour preserved).

functional.title: Accurate documentation, campaign deployment guidance and changelog
functional.description:
README.md, docs/API.md, docs/OPERATIONS.md and CHANGELOG.md must match the code. They must cover:
- API-key authentication
- the new settings
- HEAD probes
- SQLite WAL and backups
- lock behaviour
- the campaign deployment profile (single instance, SQLite, 50 RPS / p95 < 100 ms, best effort)
- the documented path to PostgreSQL for multi-worker or larger scale
acceptance_criteria: No doc says there is no authentication. README, API.md and OPERATIONS.md all describe: the X-API-Key header on /api/links*; the 401 response; fail-closed behaviour when API_KEY is unset; the 16-character minimum.

The README configuration table lists every Settings env var, including API_KEY, SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS, DB_POOL_SIZE, DB_MAX_OVERFLOW and DB_POOL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS. A test iterates over the Settings fields and checks that each env name appears in README.md.
docs/API.md documents HEAD on /healthz and /readyz and lists 401 in the error table.

docs/OPERATIONS.md documents:
- WAL and its -wal/-shm side files
- the backup procedure (sqlite3 .backup, or copying all three files while the service is stopped)
- that WAL needs a writable local directory and does not work on network filesystems
- the corrected locking runbook
- pool sizing guidance

docs/OPERATIONS.md contains a 'Campaign deployment' section with the agreed targets (up to ~50 RPS, redirect p95 < 100 ms, best effort, one instance). It gives the supported topology: one instance and one uvicorn worker on SQLite with WAL, on local disk. It gives recommended values for SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS and the pool settings, a pre-launch checklist (startup tuning log line, HEAD /readyz monitor, backup taken), and the restart and recovery steps for best-effort availability.

docs/OPERATIONS.md contains a 'Scaling beyond the campaign profile' section. It states that running several workers, several replicas or above ~50 RPS requires PostgreSQL, because SQLite stays single-writer. It also gives the migration steps: add and pin a driver (e.g. psycopg) in requirements.txt, set DATABASE_URL, create the schema on a fresh database, copy the data, and size DB_POOL_SIZE/DB_MAX_OVERFLOW per worker. It states explicitly that no driver ships in this release.
CHANGELOG.md [Unreleased] records API-key authentication, HEAD probe support, the WAL/busy_timeout and pool settings, the stats aggregation change and the MySQL collation note.

functional.title: Regression protection of existing contracts
functional.description: All existing behaviour covered by FR-1..FR-13 and NFR-1..NFR-9 must be preserved, especially on the paths this change touches.
acceptance_criteria: All 165 existing tests pass. Existing assertions are not loosened; tests may only be extended.
Redirect contract (FR-5): 307 with a Location byte-identical to the stored URL and Cache-Control: no-store; 404 JSON for unknown or malformed codes; 410 JSON with no Location for deactivated links.
Immediate deactivation (FR-7): the first GET or HEAD /{code} after DELETE /api/links/{code} returns 410.
Click recording (FR-8): exactly one click per successful GET; none for HEAD, 404 or 410; referrer truncated to 2048 characters and UA to 512; counts visible immediately.
Auth: /api/links* requires X-API-Key; redirects and probes stay public.
Idempotency and code allocation (FR-3, FR-4): uniqueness, collision retry, 503 on exhaustion and race handling all still pass on a temp SQLite file with WAL enabled.
Error contract (FR-11, NFR-3): JSON {detail} everywhere; SQLAlchemyError becomes 503; unknown errors become a generic 500; nothing internal is leaked.

non_functional.requirement: Campaign target (Q-1): at a sustained ~50 requests per second of mixed traffic on one app instance backed by a temp file SQLite database with WAL and default settings, redirects must meet p95 < 100 ms with zero 5xx. The traffic is 95% GET /{code} spread over 1,000 seeded links and 5% POST /api/links. The click_event row count must equal successful GETs minus any logged best-effort click failures (expected 0).
non_functional.measure: New tests/test_perf_concurrency.py, marked slow. It runs an open-loop, paced generator at 50 RPS for 20 s (1,000 requests) using a ThreadPoolExecutor of up to 16 workers and TestClient. It asserts the status distribution (no 5xx), a redirect p95 < 100 ms measured client-side per request, and the click count. Latency is measured in process and excludes network; the pre-launch production check is covered by NFR-20.

non_functional.requirement: The existing single-threaded budget (NFR-4) must not regress: redirect p95 < 50 ms and create p95 < 100 ms on 10k seeded links.
non_functional.measure: The existing test_performance_p95_redirect_and_create passes with its thresholds unchanged.

non_functional.requirement: A failure or lock timeout during click recording must never turn a resolvable redirect into a non-307 response. With a lock held, the worst-case added latency is bounded by SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS + 500 ms.
non_functional.measure: The lock-holding tests in FR-15, plus a fault-injection test that makes the click INSERT or COMMIT raise OperationalError and asserts a 307, a rollback, and a log line without the IP.

non_functional.requirement: Stats memory must be O(days + referrer groups), not O(clicks).
non_functional.measure: The FR-18 tracemalloc comparison (200k vs 2k clicks, peak at most 2×) and the repository return-shape test.

non_functional.requirement: NFR-1 is preserved: no raw IP is stored or logged anywhere, including the new click-failure warning logs, the startup configuration log and all error paths. ip_hash stays HMAC-SHA256 and is set only when IP_HASH_SALT is configured.
non_functional.measure: The existing privacy tests, plus a caplog test on the click-failure and lock paths asserting that the client IP string and X-Forwarded-For values are absent.

non_functional.requirement:
No security regressions:
- /healthz never touches the DB.
- Probe and redirect errors leak no exception text.
- Cache-Control: no-store stays on redirects, and no response caching or CDN headers are added.
- The API-key check stays constant-time and fails closed.
- No secrets appear in logs, including DB URLs with credentials.
non_functional.measure: The existing auth, health and error tests plus the new HEAD probe tests; static checks for eval/exec/subprocess and for text() used only with literals; and a caplog test confirming the startup log contains neither the DATABASE_URL password nor API_KEY.

non_functional.requirement:
At startup the app logs one structured line with the effective DB tuning and no credentials:
- backend dialect
- pool size, overflow and timeout
- for SQLite, journal_mode, synchronous and busy_timeout

Operators can then confirm the campaign configuration from the logs.
non_functional.measure: A caplog test on create_app with a TestClient lifespan asserts that the fields are present and the secrets absent.

non_functional.requirement:
Architecture and static rules hold:
- Layering points inward.
- Services import no FastAPI or Starlette.
- Core imports nothing from api, services or repositories.
- There are no lru_cache/cache names and no module-level caches.
- New settings are validated in app/core/config.py.
- requirements.txt stays pinned with == and gains no new runtime dependency (no database driver, per Q-2).

Test coverage stays at or above 99%, and every new test docstring names the FR/NFR ids it covers.
non_functional.measure: The existing AST and static architecture tests (NFR-2, NFR-6, NFR-9) pass; pytest --cov reports ≥ 99%; and a test or review confirms that requirements.txt contains no new entries compared with the baseline.

non_functional.requirement: No schema changes to existing tables (links, click_events, idempotency_keys), other than the MySQL-only collation declaration, which affects only fresh MySQL databases and comes with documented DDL. The deployed SQLite database keeps working with no manual steps.
non_functional.measure: A test compiles CreateTable for SQLite and PostgreSQL and compares it with a baseline snapshot. A second test starts the app against a SQLite file created by the previous version (rollback-journal mode) and confirms it switches to WAL and serves redirects and stats successfully.

non_functional.requirement: Burst headroom above the campaign target (TV-ad spikes): with unpaced load from 16 concurrent client threads, 2,000 requests total in the same 95/5 GET/POST mix on a temp file SQLite database with WAL, there must be zero 5xx responses and redirect p95 < 250 ms in CI. Clicks may be dropped only through logged best-effort failures.
non_functional.measure: A second case in tests/test_perf_concurrency.py, marked slow. It asserts no 5xx, the p95 bound, and that the click count plus the logged click failures equals the successful GETs.

non_functional.requirement: Before launch, operators can verify the campaign target on the real deployment without new tooling. The documented checklist covers: the startup tuning log line, HEAD /healthz and HEAD /readyz returning 200, a recent backup, and a short smoke load at ~50 RPS against a test link showing p95 < 100 ms.
non_functional.measure: Reviewers confirm the checklist is present in the 'Campaign deployment' section of docs/OPERATIONS.md (FR-20). A doc test checks that the section exists and mentions the HEAD probes and the targets.

ambiguities.question: What are the measurable campaign targets: expected peak redirect requests per second or concurrent visitors, the redirect latency target (p95/p99), and the availability goal during the campaign window?
ambiguities.why: The target decides the architecture. Modest load can be met with the WAL, pool and lean-query changes in this spec. Medium load needs PostgreSQL. Large load needs caching and asynchronous click ingestion.
options: Modest: up to about 50 RPS, p95 < 100 ms, best effort (one instance is enough)
Medium: about 500 RPS, p95 < 100 ms, 99.9% availability (needs PostgreSQL and several workers)
Large: several thousand RPS or TV-spike bursts (needs PostgreSQL, multiple replicas, possibly an edge cache and an asynchronous click pipeline)
ambiguities.default: Modest: up to about 50 RPS, p95 < 100 ms, best effort on one instance. Encoded in NFR-10 (target), NFR-19 (burst headroom) and NFR-20 (pre-launch verification).
ambiguities.resolved_by: Modest: up to about 50 RPS, p95 < 100 ms, best effort (one instance is enough)

ambiguities.question: Which database and topology will serve the campaign in production: SQLite on one instance, or PostgreSQL/MySQL with several workers or replicas? If PostgreSQL, should we pin a driver (e.g. psycopg) in requirements.txt?
ambiguities.why: SQLite stays single-writer even with WAL. PostgreSQL would need a pinned driver and validated pool defaults, and multiple instances would rule out any in-process cache.
options: SQLite, one instance, one worker
SQLite with several workers (not recommended)
PostgreSQL with several workers/replicas, and a pinned driver added
MySQL with several workers/replicas, and a pinned driver added
ambiguities.default: Keep SQLite on one instance with one worker, hardened with WAL, busy_timeout and a configurable pool. Add no driver. Document the PostgreSQL migration path (FR-15, FR-16, FR-20, NFR-17).
ambiguities.resolved_by: Keep the current SQLite backend and harden it (WAL, busy_timeout, configurable pool). Add no new driver. Document the move to PostgreSQL for multi-worker or campaign scale.

ambiguities.question: What does 'more trustworthy' mean to marketing: reliable redirects and monitoring, accurate click analytics, safe links (protection against phishing and malicious destinations), or easy-to-type and recognisable links (vanity aliases, codes without confusable characters, a branded domain)?
ambiguities.why: Each extra option is a separate product feature with its own API, data and test changes. They add to this spec rather than conflict with it, but they compete for the one-week window.
options: Reliability, monitoring, accurate analytics and correct docs (this spec)
Plus link safety: destination allow/deny lists or malware scanning
Plus human-friendly links: vanity aliases or an alphabet without confusable characters for new codes
Plus a human-friendly HTML 404/410 page for browsers
ambiguities.default: Trustworthy means: redirects that keep working under load, probes that report the truth, bounded and accurate stats, case-correct matching, and docs that match the code. The other options are out of scope for this release.

ambiguities.question: May we cache redirect lookups in process to gain speed, accepting a staleness window after deactivation?
ambiguities.why: A cache conflicts with the immediate-410 contract (FR-7), which matters for phishing takedowns. With the modest target (Q-1), it is unnecessary.
options: No cache (deactivation is always immediate)
Per-app cache with a short TTL, invalidated on DELETE in the same process
Shared cache (e.g. Redis), with a new dependency and infrastructure
ambiguities.default: No redirect cache in this release. The 50 RPS / p95 < 100 ms target is met through WAL, the narrow lookup and pool sizing.

ambiguities.question: Should click recording move off the request path (background task, batching, queue) to reduce latency?
ambiguities.why: An asynchronous design changes the click-count visibility contract and existing tests, and risks losing clicks or leaking IPs in buffers.
options: Keep it synchronous and best-effort (counts visible immediately)
Asynchronous or batched, with a flush on shutdown (possible loss on crash; counts eventually consistent)
ambiguities.default: Keep it synchronous and best-effort, with lock waits bounded by SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS. This is sufficient at ~50 RPS on SQLite with WAL.

ambiguities.question: Should clicks from link-preview bots and crawlers be excluded from or flagged in the campaign analytics?
ambiguities.why: Social and messaging link previews inflate counts. Flagging needs a schema change to click_events, which create_all will not apply to deployed databases.
options: Count all GETs (current behaviour)
Flag bots using a User-Agent heuristic (needs a new column and a migration)
Exclude bots from counts
ambiguities.default: Keep the current counting semantics and document that counts include automated GETs.

ambiguities.question: Under a held write lock, should the redirect give up on the click quickly (drop it) or wait longer to record it?
ambiguities.why: This decides the default and the recommended campaign value for SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS: visitor latency under contention versus analytics completeness.
options: Short wait, e.g. 200–1000 ms (faster redirect, may drop clicks under contention)
Current 5000 ms default (fewer dropped clicks, slower redirects under contention)
ambiguities.default: Code default stays 5000 ms to preserve current behaviour. The campaign deployment section recommends 1000 ms on SQLite, given the p95 < 100 ms target.

ambiguities.question: Is MySQL actually used anywhere, and are operators able to run the documented ALTER TABLE on existing MySQL databases before the campaign?
ambiguities.why: Changing the model only affects fresh databases. Since production is SQLite (Q-2), this only matters for other deployments.
options: Not used: declare the model collation and document the DDL only
Used: the DDL must be run as a deployment step before launch
ambiguities.default: Not used for the campaign. Declare the binary collation in the model and document the DDL, with no automatic migration. FR-19 is a 'could'.

ambiguities.question: Who runs the pre-launch smoke check (~50 RPS for a short period) against the production instance, and with what tool?
ambiguities.why: The in-process CI tests (NFR-10, NFR-19) exclude network and host differences. Only a check on the real host confirms the p95 < 100 ms target.
options: Operations runs it with an existing load tool against a dedicated test link
Skip it and rely on the CI tests and startup log verification
ambiguities.default: Operations runs it with their existing tooling, following the checklist in OPERATIONS.md (NFR-20). No load tool is added to this repository.

assumptions: The production campaign profile is one app instance with one uvicorn worker, SQLite on local disk with WAL, up to ~50 RPS, redirect p95 < 100 ms, and best-effort availability (Q-1, Q-2).
New requirement ids continue from the existing FR-1..FR-13 and NFR-1..NFR-9, which the current tests reference. Those requirements stay in force and are protected by FR-21.
Errors stay JSON-only ({"detail": ...}). No HTML error pages are introduced.
There is no migration tooling. Schema changes to existing tables are avoided, except the MySQL-only collation declaration (FR-19), which affects only fresh databases and comes with documented DDL.

WAL, synchronous=NORMAL and busy_timeout are applied through a SQLAlchemy connect event, and only for file-based SQLite. Enabling WAL on an existing rollback-journal database file is automatic and persistent.
Engine, pool and settings stay per app (created in create_app and stored on app.state), so tests stay isolated.
No new runtime dependencies are added (in particular, no PostgreSQL or MySQL driver), and no network calls are made to third-party services.
CI latency checks run in process through TestClient and exclude network latency. Production confirmation is the pre-launch smoke check (NFR-20).
Concurrency and large-volume tests are marked slow. The existing NFR-4 thresholds are unchanged.
The stats endpoint keeps its current window and validation contract (days 1..365) and its response schema.
Load-balancer, TLS, CDN and process-supervisor (restart) configuration is managed outside this codebase.
out_of_scope: Redirect response caching (in process, shared, CDN or browser). Cache-Control: no-store is kept.
Asynchronous, batched or queued click ingestion.
Bot or crawler detection and filtering of clicks.
Vanity or custom aliases, branded domains, and changes to the code alphabet for new codes.
HTML landing or error pages for browsers.
Rate limiting and DDoS protection (handled at the gateway or edge).
Link-safety scanning or destination reputation checks.
Migration tooling, denormalised click counters, and new indexes on existing tables.
Adding a PostgreSQL or MySQL driver to requirements.txt, and actually migrating production to PostgreSQL. Only the documentation of that path is in scope (Q-2).
Multi-worker or multi-replica deployment on SQLite, high availability, failover and multi-region infrastructure.
Load targets above ~50 RPS, and availability SLOs beyond best effort.
Changing expire_on_commit or removing the extra refresh SELECT after create.
A load-testing tool or harness for production in this repository.

risks.description: TV ads produce sharp bursts that may briefly exceed the agreed ~50 RPS. SQLite with one write per click is single-writer, so bursts can raise latency or drop clicks.
risks.mitigation: Click writes are best-effort with a bounded busy_timeout (FR-15, NFR-12), and redirects never fail because of a click write. NFR-19 checks burst headroom (16 concurrent clients, zero 5xx). OPERATIONS.md recommends SQLITE_BUSY_TIMEOUT_MS=1000 for the campaign and documents the PostgreSQL path for anything larger.

risks.description: Enabling WAL changes the on-disk files and the backup procedure. It fails on network filesystems and may not apply to in-memory test databases.
risks.mitigation: Apply WAL only to file-based SQLite and tolerate in-memory URLs. Add a pragma verification test and an upgrade test from a rollback-journal file (NFR-18). Update the backup and runbook sections of OPERATIONS.md (FR-20).

risks.description: Rewriting stats as SQL aggregation could subtly change UTC-day bucketing or window edges across dialects.
risks.mitigation: Keep the existing stats tests unmodified as the equivalence oracle. Guard dialect-specific expressions and compile them for SQLite, PostgreSQL and MySQL. Streaming with yield_per is an acceptable fallback.

risks.description: Changing probe routing to support HEAD could disturb the catch-all order, the OpenAPI paths or the 405 behaviour, or make /healthz touch the DB.
risks.mitigation: Use api_route(methods=['GET','HEAD']) on the probes and keep the redirect router last. Assert the 405, no DB access, unchanged HEAD /{code} behaviour and the OpenAPI path set (FR-14).

risks.description: Short busy timeouts drop clicks under contention, which reduces analytics completeness during the campaign.
risks.mitigation: Make the timeout configurable (Q-7) and log each dropped click without the IP so drops can be counted. Document the trade-off.

risks.description: The concurrent and paced load tests could be flaky on slow CI runners, particularly the p95 < 100 ms assertion.
risks.mitigation: Mark the tests slow, use an open-loop paced generator at the target rate rather than saturating load, treat zero 5xx as the primary assertion, and keep the stricter burst threshold generous (250 ms).

risks.description: The MySQL collation fix does not reach existing deployments without the manual DDL.
risks.mitigation: Production is SQLite (Q-2). Document the exact ALTER TABLE in OPERATIONS.md and the CHANGELOG.

risks.description: The one-week deadline leaves little room for review and staged rollout before a high-visibility launch.
risks.mitigation: Prioritise the must items (FR-14, FR-15, FR-16, FR-18, FR-20, FR-21), then FR-17, then FR-19. Keep every change behind defaults that preserve current behaviour. Run the NFR-20 pre-launch checklist on the production host.

risks.description: Best-effort availability on one instance means any host or process failure is a full outage during the campaign, and SQLite data loss is possible without backups.
risks.mitigation: This is accepted per Q-1. OPERATIONS.md documents a process-supervisor restart policy, HEAD /readyz external monitoring (FR-14), WAL-safe backups before launch, and the recovery steps.

risks.description: Operators might start several uvicorn workers on SQLite to 'go faster', which increases write-lock contention.
risks.mitigation: The 'Campaign deployment' section states one worker on SQLite and points to the PostgreSQL migration path for multi-worker setups. The NFR-16 startup log makes the configuration visible.
